title: XML Media Types
summary: Standardizes the media types text/xml, application/xml, and related types for exchanging XML, plus the +xml suffix convention for naming XML-based types. It tells software how to label and handle XML content. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 7303.

plainLanguage.summary:
A media type is the label that says what kind of data a message carries, such as text/plain or image/jpeg. This RFC adds the labels for XML and fixes the rule for the character set that goes with them.

It also adds a convention: a format built on XML should end its name with plus xml, so that any program that understands XML can spot it and open it.

questions: what is the mime type for xml
what is the default charset for text/xml
subtitle: The official media type labels for XML, plus the +xml suffix for naming XML-based formats.

tldr.problem: Software needs a label to say what a chunk of data is, and the labels for XML did not exist. The older SGML labels were not a good fit, since many programs can read XML but not SGML.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers five media types for XML content and sets out a naming convention, the +xml suffix, so that a program can recognise any XML-based format and hand it to an XML processor.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard and was later replaced by RFC 7303. When it was published it obsoleted RFC 2376 and updated the MIME media type registration process in RFC 2048.

today: RFC 3023 was a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 7303. When it was published it obsoleted RFC 2376 and updated RFC 2048, the procedure for registering MIME media types.

sections.title: Why XML Needs Its Own Media Types
sections.content:
The World Wide Web Consortium has issued XML 1.0, and to enable the exchange of XML network entities this document standardizes five media types: text/xml, application/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-dtd. It also standardizes a convention, using the suffix +xml, for naming media types outside these five when they represent XML MIME entities.

XML entities are currently exchanged on the World Wide Web, and XML is also used for property values and parameter marshalling by the WebDAV protocol for remote web authoring, so there is a need for a media type that properly labels the exchange of XML network entities.

Although XML is a subset of SGML, which has the media types text/sgml and application/sgml, the RFC gives several reasons why those are inappropriate for XML. There are many applications that can process XML but cannot process SGML, because SGML has a larger feature set. SGML applications cannot always process XML entities, because XML uses features of recent technical corrigenda to SGML. And the definition of text/sgml and application/sgml includes parameters for SGML bit combination transformation format and SGML boot attribute, which XML does not use, so it would be ambiguous if such parameters were given for an XML entity.

Because XML is an integral part of the WebDAV protocol and World Wide Web Consortium Recommendations have conventionally been assigned IETF tree media types, the XML media types belong in the IETF media types tree. Since XML will also be used as a foundation for other media types in every branch of that tree, media types based on XML that are not identified as text/xml or application/xml should be named with the suffix +xml. This lets XML-based tools, browsers, editors and search engines, work with all XML-based media types.
sections.plainLanguage: SGML was the parent language, but XML is a smaller, stricter version of it, and many programs understand XML without understanding SGML. So XML needed its own labels rather than borrowing its parent's.

sections.title: The Five Media Types and When to Use Them
sections.content:
Within the XML specification, XML MIME entities can be classified into four types, called document entities, external DTD subsets, external parsed entities and external parameter entities. The media types text/xml and application/xml may be used for document entities. The media type text/xml-external-parsed-entity or application/xml-external-parsed-entity should be used for external parsed entities, and application/xml-dtd should be used for external DTD subsets or external parameter entities. Application/xml and text/xml must not be used for external parameter entities or external DTD subsets, and must not be used for external parsed entities unless they are also well-formed document entities and are referenced as such. The RFC that this one obsoletes allowed such usage, although in practice it was likely to have been rare.

If an XML document is readable by casual users, text/xml is preferable to application/xml. MIME user agents and web user agents that do not have explicit support for text/xml will treat it as text/plain, for example by displaying the entity as plain text. Application/xml is preferable when the XML entity is unreadable by casual users, and the same distinction applies between text/xml-external-parsed-entity and application/xml-external-parsed-entity. The RFC adds a note that users are not used to text containing tags and often find such tags disorienting or annoying, so the conservative principle is to use application/* rather than text/* when in doubt, so as not to put information in front of users that they will quite likely not understand.

The top-level media type text has restrictions on MIME entities, in particular that the UTF-16 family, UCS-4 and UTF-32 are not allowed, except over HTTP, which uses a MIME-like mechanism. An XML document or external parsed entity encoded in those character encodings therefore cannot be labeled as text/xml or text/xml-external-parsed-entity, except for HTTP.

The two families differ when the charset parameter is not specified. If the default charset for text/xml, which is US-ASCII, is inconvenient for some reason, application/xml provides an alternative. The rules in short form are these. For text/xml, text/xml-external-parsed-entity and XML-based types under the text top-level type: the charset parameter is strongly recommended; if it is not specified the default is us-ascii, and the default of iso-8859-1 in HTTP is explicitly overridden; there are no error handling provisions; and an encoding declaration, if present, is irrelevant, but when saving a received resource as a file the correct encoding declaration should be inserted. For application/xml, application/xml-external-parsed-entity, application/xml-dtd and XML-based types under other top-level types: the charset parameter is strongly recommended and, if present, takes precedence; and if the parameter is omitted, conforming XML processors must follow the requirements in section 4.3.3 of the XML specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is simple: use the text version when a person is likely to read the markup, and the application version when they are not.

sections.title: Charsets and the Byte Order Mark
sections.content:
The charset parameter is strongly recommended, because it lets XML processors determine the character encoding of the entity authoritatively. The recommended value is utf-8, which is supported by all conforming processors of XML. If the entity is transmitted via HTTP, which is exempt from the restrictions on the text top-level type, utf-16 is also recommended, and it too is supported by all conforming processors of XML. Since handling CR, LF and NUL for text types in most MIME applications would cause undesired transformations of individual octets in UTF-16 multi-octet characters, gateways from HTTP to those MIME applications must transform the entity from text/xml with charset utf-16 to application/xml with charset utf-16.

The RFC gives several reasons why the charset parameter is authoritative. Some MIME processing engines do transcoding of bodies of the text top-level type without reference to the internal content, so an agent might change text/xml with charset iso-2022-jp to text/xml with charset utf-8 without modifying the encoding declaration of the document. And text/xml must be compatible with text/plain, since MIME agents that do not understand text/xml fall back to handling it as text/plain; if the charset parameter were not authoritative, that fallback would cause data corruption. The RFC notes the inconsistency with HTTP/1.1, which uses ISO-8859-1 as its default for a historical reason, and says US-ASCII was chosen for XML because it is the intersection of UTF-8 and ISO-8859-1 and is already used by MIME. Because the charset parameter is authoritative, the charset is not always declared inside an XML encoding declaration, so special care is needed when the recipient strips the MIME header and stores the entity persistently. Unless the charset is UTF-8 or UTF-16, the recipient should also store information about the charset, perhaps by embedding a correct XML encoding declaration.

XML MIME entities in the charset utf-16 must begin with a byte order mark, the octet sequence 0xFE 0xFF, or 0xFF 0xFE depending on endianness. The BOM is an encoding signature and is not part of either the markup or the character data. Applications converting XML from utf-16 to a non-Unicode encoding must strip the BOM before converting, and when converting into utf-16 the BOM must be added after the conversion is complete. The charsets utf-16le and utf-16be prohibit the BOM: an entity encoded in either must not begin with it but should contain an encoding declaration.
sections.plainLanguage: The label says how the bytes are encoded, and it wins over anything written inside the document. That matters when a program copies the document around and changes its encoding without noticing.

sections.title: The +xml Suffix Convention
sections.content:
The document recommends a suffix of +xml for identifying XML-based MIME media types, whatever their particular content may represent. This allows generic XML processors and technologies to be used on a wide variety of different XML document types at a minimum cost, using the existing frameworks for media type registration. Although the use of a suffix was not part of the original MIME architecture, the RFC considers that it provides the most functionality with the least potential for interoperability problems.

As XML development continues, new XML document types appear rapidly, and many would benefit from the more specific identification that a particular MIME media type provides. But all XML documents share common structures and syntax that make common processing possible. The areas where generic processing is useful include browsing, since an XML browser can display any XML document with a provided CSS or XSLT style sheet whatever the vocabulary; editing, since any XML editor can read, modify and save any XML document; fragment identification with XPointers; hypertext linking with XLink; searching, since XML-oriented search engines and web crawlers should be able to read XML documents even if ignorant of the particular vocabulary; storage in XML-oriented systems; and well-formedness and validity checking.

When a new media type is introduced for an XML-based format, the name should end with +xml. Applications may match types that represent XML MIME entities by comparing the subtype to the pattern */*+xml, although the RFC notes that HTTP does not support Accept headers of that form, so it must not be used in that way. Four of the five media types in this document also represent XML MIME entities while not conforming to the pattern.

Generic processing is not always appropriate. The authors of some media types may wish their types to remain entirely opaque except to applications designed for them, and by not following the naming convention they can avoid XML-generic processing. Registrars SHOULD follow the convention unless there is a particularly compelling reason not to, and media subtypes that do not represent XML MIME entities must not be allowed to register with a +xml suffix. Registrations under the text top-level type should define their charset parameter and encoding considerations as the same as text/xml, and registrations under other top-level types as the same as application/xml.
sections.plainLanguage: The suffix is a signal. A browser or a search engine can see it, know the content is XML, and process it without having to know what the particular format means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
XML, as a subset of SGML, has all of the same security considerations as specified in RFC 1874, and likely more, due to its expected ubiquitous deployment. XML MIME entities contain information to be parsed and processed by the recipient's XML system, and these entities may contain, and such systems may permit, explicit system level commands to be executed while processing the data. To the extent that an XML system will execute arbitrary command strings, recipients of XML entities may be at risk. In general it may be possible to specify commands that perform unauthorized file operations or make changes to the display processor's environment.

Any information stored outside the direct control of the user, including CSS style sheets, XSL transformations, entity declarations and DTDs, can be a source of insecurity. A small modification made to a master style sheet could make words in critical locations disappear in user documents, without directly modifying the user document or the style sheet it references. The security of any XML document is therefore vitally dependent on all of the documents recursively referenced by that document.

The simplest attack adds declarations that break validation. Extraneous declarations to a list of character entities can break the contract used by documents, and a tiny change that produces a fatal error in a DTD could halt XML processing on a large scale. More sophisticated tricks, such as changing attributes from being optional to required, are difficult to track down, and the most dangerous option available is redefining default values for attributes: if developers have relied on defaulted attributes for security, a relatively small change might expose enormous quantities of information. Another option is entity spoofing, which can insert text into documents. Because XML 1.0 permits multiple entity declarations and the first declaration takes precedence, it is possible to insert malicious content where an entity is used. The RFC also notes that XML may have some of the same security concerns as plain text, since escape sequences can change the display environment, and that display processors should either filter such material or reset important settings after a display operation is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: An XML document can pull in other documents, and the damage is often in those rather than in the document itself. A style sheet that everyone trusts can be edited to change what a reader sees.

viz.caption: The five media types this RFC registers

items.title: text/xml
items.text: For XML documents that casual users can read. Agents without XML support fall back to plain text.

items.title: application/xml
items.text: For XML documents that are not meant to be read as text by casual users.

items.title: text/xml-external-parsed-entity
items.text: For an external parsed entity that casual users can read.

items.title: application/xml-external-parsed-entity
items.text: For an external parsed entity where a plain text display is inappropriate.

items.title: application/xml-dtd
items.text: For an external DTD subset or an external parameter entity.
